groups.title: Streams & Backpressure
groups.question: Explain how streams help a Node.js service handle large amounts of data.

followUps.Readable & Writable Streams: Why does streaming a large file use far less memory than reading it into a Buffer?
followUps.Backpressure & pipe(): What happens to memory if you ignore the return value of write() on a slow destination?

evidence.text: Streams process data in small chunks as it arrives instead of loading all of it at once.
Memory stays roughly constant whatever the file size, while reading the whole file into a Buffer needs memory for all of it.

notEnough: Only saying streams are for big data without explaining chunks or memory.

evidence.text: write() returns false when the destination's buffer is full, meaning stop and wait for the drain event.
Ignoring that keeps the data piling up in memory until the process runs out of it.
pipe() and stream.pipeline handle this automatically by pausing the source until the destination catches up.

notEnough: Only naming backpressure without explaining what happens when it's ignored.

groups.title: Async Iteration
groups.question: Walk through how you build and consume a data pipeline in Node.js without messy event handlers.

followUps.Async Iterators & for-await-of: How does for-await-of make reading a stream simpler and safer than data and end events?
followUps.Transform Streams: What makes a Transform stream pipeline hang forever, and how do you avoid it?

evidence.text: Readable streams are async iterable, so for await...of reads them chunk by chunk like a loop.
It replaces separate data, end and error handlers with one loop, and stream errors become exceptions you can catch with try/catch.
The loop only asks for the next chunk when the current one is done, which gives backpressure for free.

notEnough: Only saying for-await-of is cleaner without saying what it replaces.

evidence.text: A Transform stream is both readable and writable, changing each chunk as it passes through, like compressing or parsing.
Its transform function must call the callback for every chunk; if it doesn't, or nobody reads the output, the pipeline stalls.
stream.pipeline connects the steps and passes any error to one handler, so a failed step doesn't leave the others hanging.

notEnough: Only saying transform streams modify data without explaining how a pipeline hangs.

groups.title: Worker Threads
groups.question: Explain how you use more than one CPU core in a Node.js application.

followUps.Worker Threads for CPU Work: When would you move work to a worker thread instead of keeping it on the main thread?
followUps.Cluster Module & Load Distribution: Why must session state live outside the process when you run a Node.js cluster?

evidence.text: CPU-heavy work on the main thread blocks the event loop, so all requests wait.
Worker threads run JavaScript on other threads, so heavy work like image processing or big calculations doesn't block the loop.
I/O-bound work doesn't need workers, because Node already handles it asynchronously.

notEnough: Only saying worker threads run things in parallel without saying when to use them.

misconceptions.text: Says worker threads make database or network calls faster.

evidence.text: The cluster module starts several Node processes, usually one per CPU core, sharing the same port.
Each process has its own memory, so a session kept in one process's memory isn't there for requests that land on another.
Session state must live in a shared store like Redis or a database.

notEnough: Only saying cluster uses all cores without explaining the memory problem.

groups.title: Error Handling in Async Code
groups.question: Explain how you make sure async errors in a Node.js server are caught and traceable.

followUps.Unhandled Promise Rejections: What happens in modern Node.js when a rejected promise has no catch, and how do you guard against it?
followUps.async_hooks & Context Propagation: How does AsyncLocalStorage let you carry a request ID through async calls?

evidence.text: In modern Node, an unhandled promise rejection crashes the process by default.
Every promise needs a catch or a try/catch around its await, and route handlers need their async errors passed to the error handler.
A process-level unhandledRejection handler is for logging and a clean shutdown, not for continuing as if nothing happened.

notEnough: Only saying always catch errors without explaining what happens to unhandled rejections.

misconceptions.text: Says an unhandled rejection only prints a warning and the process keeps running normally.

evidence.text: AsyncLocalStorage keeps a value, like a request ID, available through all the async calls started from one request.
Code deep in the call chain reads it without passing it through every function's parameters.
Loggers use it to attach the request ID to every log line, so one request can be traced.

notEnough: Only naming async_hooks or AsyncLocalStorage without explaining what it carries.
